title: Conditioning on a Count, and on Shared Trials
quickIdea: When the condition is an event about a random variable, write the ratio P(Y = y and C)/P(C) and count outcomes. When the two events share trials, break the count at the shared trial instead of assuming independence.
remember: Given X3 = 0, any function of X3 is constant, so Y = X1X2 XOR X3 collapses to Y = X1X2 and the question becomes P(X1X2 = 0) = 3/4.

Enumerate when the space is small. Eight equally likely triples for GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.37; sixty-four toss sequences for GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.53, or twenty-four once the condition fixes two of the four tosses.
In GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.53 the events share toss 2, so they are not independent and P(E1)P(E2) is not available; the answer 1/2 comes from counting twelve favourable completions out of twenty-four.
Conditioning on a symmetric event usually leaves the remaining trials uniform, which is why the answer can coincide with the unconditional one - as it does here.
A function of independent variables is independent of a function of the others, which is the licence to simplify P(Y = 0 | X3 = 0) into P(X1X2 = 0).
Never multiply two events that share a trial. Check which trials each event uses before reaching for the product rule.

example.prompt: X1, X2, X3 are independent, each 0 or 1 with probability 1/2. Y = X1X2 XOR X3. Find P(Y = 0 | X3 = 0).
example.work: With X3 = 0 the XOR is the identity, so Y = 0 exactly when X1X2 = 0, that is for (0,0), (0,1) and (1,0): three of the four equally likely pairs. By the definition, P(Y = 0 and X3 = 0) = 3/8 and P(X3 = 0) = 4/8, so the ratio is 3/4.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.37 collapses a function of the conditioned variable; GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.53 conditions on an event that shares a toss with the event asked about. Both are the definition plus counting, and neither is a product of independent probabilities.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.37: X1, X2, X3 are i.i.d. with P(Xi = 0) = P(Xi = 1) = 1/2 and Y = X1X2 XOR X3. Then P(Y = 0 | X3 = 0) = ____.
variations.why: Three of the four pairs (X1, X2) make X1X2 = 0, so the conditional probability is 3/4.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.53 (Q.63 in the official paper): an unbiased coin is tossed 6 times. E1 = at least two heads among tosses 2, 4, 6. E2 = equal numbers of heads and tails among tosses 1, 2, 3, 5. Find P(E1 | E2) to one decimal place.
variations.why: E2 fixes two heads and two tails among tosses 1, 2, 3, 5: 6 patterns out of 16, and tosses 4 and 6 are free, giving 24 equally likely completions. Of those, 12 satisfy E1: 3 patterns x 3 completions where toss 2 is a head, plus 3 x 1 where toss 2 is a tail. So the probability is 12/24.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: In GATE CSE 2026 Set 2 Q.53, why is P(E1)P(E2) not the numerator?
variations.answer: Because E1 and E2 share toss 2, so they are not independent and the joint probability is not the product.
variations.why: P(E1) = 1/2 and P(E2) = 6/16, whose product is 3/16; the true joint probability is 12/64 = 3/16. The numbers coincide here by symmetry, which is exactly why the counting argument is the safe route.

trap.what: Multiplying two probabilities that share a trial, or forgetting that a function of the conditioned variable becomes constant.
trap.why: Sharing a trial makes the events dependent in general, so the product rule does not apply; and conditioning on X3 = 0 removes X3 from the expression entirely.
trap.counterexample: In GATE CSE 2015 Set 3 Q.37 the naive product P(Y = 0)P(X3 = 0) would be (1/2)(1/2) = 1/4, while the joint probability is 3/8 - the events are dependent because both involve X3.

check.question: Three fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of exactly two heads, given at least one head?
check.explanation: Seven of the eight outcomes have at least one head, and three of those (HHT, HTH, THH) have exactly two, so the conditional probability is 3/7.
